Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: Sign language names actually just any other name used in sign language. It's in hearing culture, we use long flowing names, or shortened names. In sign language, you typically use a one or two or three-handed shape. There's like 100 different ones that are in use. So when someone first meets a hearing person, they'll learn their name in sign language. And then over time, once you become friends, you'll watch their movements and you'll see like, oh, this guy really likes contracting his fingers inward. So maybe his name is a claw name, or this person has really pointy features on their face, so we'll make her a face-shape name. And then over time it becomes just solidified. You just give a name. I think that that's really the fun thing.

Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: Names in sign language are two or three gestures that represent a person or place and have an iconic, arbitrary, or modified classifier origin. Iconic signs have some relationship to a quality or behaviour of the person, for instance, my name is a mockery of my grandfather's broken nose and broken glasses. Places like London or Dublin have iconic signs also. The arbitrary ones are modified versions of an existing sign, e.g. for my surname sign I take the sign for father and modify it. All those then have glosses e.g. grandad nose. People learn name signs for their friends, family, special people, celebrities etc. Some work in the deaf world has names, some don't. Signing a name sign can be an address and its use is personal choice as can the signing of the name signs of others. If you use a name for someone casually without intro, it may be offensive to some.

Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: Sign language has its own way of making names. It's not just dictionary-words signed very fast. We have a set of rules about how to make or choose a name sign for someone, which could be initials, some characteristic, a pun. A lot of it is just cultural. Also a lot of things are semantically based. For example: Chinese name Zhang, or Chang, is a spear, a weapon. So I know and sign Chinese names are very different from Indian names. English names, the same word is very good or bad for signing. Hannah, nice name to sign, Alex is also good. And then there's Eustacia, that's horrible to sign. Some people I don't even bother giving a name sign, I just use their initials because they just have horrible names. So it's a very fluid, flexible system.

Question: How do the mammals of the ocean hydrate themselves.
items.raw:
Hi Tom,

Thanks for your question, nice to hear from you.

There's two ways that marine mammals hydrate themselves. First is that they just eat water or actually eat preys that are very high in water content. So a whale eats a ton of krill, for example, and the krill are very high in water, and that's actually where most of their hydration comes from. For those of them that drink water directly, that's actually a problem because seawater has a very high salt concentration. And in order to drink seawater and actually hydrate, they have to separate the salt from the water somehow. So all marine mammals have very efficient kidneys that can remove very high amounts of salt. Some of them also have dedicated salt glands. For example, seals have these nasal glands where they just cry out the salt. And for some birds, that's also very common, they have these glands next to their beaks. So basically, they hydrate themselves in two ways. One, by eating very water rich prey, and two by drinking seawater or brackish water, and then removing the salt, the salt from the water either through their kidneys or through salt glands.

Question: why child support is based on income rather than what a child would need monthly.
items.raw: Child support formulas don't aim to reproduce exactly what each child would need, but they're supposed to approximate the child's share of the family budget while the parents were together. And so they factor in incomes and number of kids and their age, etc. So income is a proxy for what each family will need. But nothing in law is perfect. You can argue for upping the support of kids that need a lot of money, say a medical condition, etc. That's what deviation motions are for. People tend to use these guidelines because they're neutral. By neutral I mean that parents can't game the formula (or rather not easily). If the amount is based on individual subjective needs of each child, then one parent will always argue for a lot more while the other argues for a lot less. And that's what guideline formulas are trying to avoid.

Question: why child support is based on income rather than what a child would need monthly.
items.raw: The reason is that the cost of a child is incredibly variable. Child support has to be predictable and enforceable, and it's very difficult to say exactly what a child needs. You don't want a contest on what your kids actually need and a fight over receipts, so instead you take a proxy variable that is relatively easy to establish, which is income. And then you say for this level of income and this number of children, the percentage is going to be whatever. That's why every state has these guidelines. But obviously that's a blunt instrument. Income doesn't necessarily correlate very well with cost of living. In Manhattan, a millionaire's income might buy a lot less than if you're in rural Alabama, but that's still the very easiest and most predictable variable, especially if you look at the alternative of contending over what the child needs and where their needs are going to be met.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.raw:
I think about popcorn in a very physical way, sometimes in a very scary way, but it's actually not that complicated. So the kernel itself is a very compressed state of starch and water. There's a very dense starch, surrounded by a very hard shell. Inside the kernel, there's a bit of water that's trapped in that shell. So when you heat up the kernel, the water turns into steam, and because it's trapped in a very hard shell, the steam builds up pressure inside the kernel. And then once the pressure is high enough, somewhere around 135 psi, the shell cracks. So all that pressure in the shell is released very, very quickly. And when the pressure is released very quickly, the steam is very energetic, and it expands the starch into a very fluffy foam. So the starch goes from being very dense to very fluffy, and it traps that steam inside the popcorn, making it very light.

I think it's an awesome concept, a very beautiful transformation from a very dense state to a very fluffy state. And I think there's a lot that we can learn from popcorn. And in my life, I know that people sometimes will call me 'popping' when I want to say "no" to them, because I have my issues like many people. And I think that the fact that we have that hard shell, that's very protective, that sometimes protects us from the world. And that shell, what it does, it also lets pressure build up inside, and then eventually you break open, and it releases pressure. And that's a good thing.

I mean, we can talk about cooking popcorn on a stovetop. And it's interesting to note that, if you have the humidity in the air around you, the popcorn will absorb moisture. The starch will actually absorb moisture, and it will become very sticky. And the popcorn will turn into a gummy mess. So what happens is the popcorn will suck up all the moisture from the air and the starch will absorb the moisture and make it very gummy. And it's really hard to cook popcorn in a very humid climate. I live in Dallas, which has very dry air, and I've noticed that my popcorn always comes out very fluffy, and it's very nice. In Seattle, I was very disappointed with popcorn. It was very bad popcorn, very dense and sticky. So it's important that you have very dry air around your popcorn.

Write a personal blog post of about 400 words prompted by the question below. Take a position and explain it with concrete detail. Plain prose, no headings or lists.

Question: When popcorn is popping, what is actually happening to the kernel inside?
items.raw:
I think popcorn is one of the most interesting phenomena from a chemical physics perspective because we end up cooking a little piece of structure under pressure. So you have this seed, which is mostly carbohydrates, starch, and protein. And then it has a hard shell. And a little bit of water that is trapped in the starch. And when we heat it up, that water starts to boil. And that water becomes steam, and it creates pressure. And that pressure basically bursts the starch into foam. So the starch is more or less expanded into a foam, and that foam is trapped inside that shell, and the shell breaks. And then the foam collapses onto itself. And that's why popcorn is what it looks like. It's basically a foam that has collapsed.

And then there is a very strong correlation between the initial moisture content of that seed and the final expansion. So if you take the seeds and you dry them down, say, to 10 percent water content, then they don't expand very much. You need about 14 percent water content for good expansion. If you get above that, they expand too much and they just break, and they become popcorn chaff. And then if you cook it too hot, it burns. So it's a very narrow range of temperature. And people say, no, no, it breaks at 180 degrees Celsius, but in my lab we looked at it more in detail. And it breaks at 160 or 165 degrees Celsius. So we do these tests with ultrasound, and we see the foam collapse, and then it expands a little bit and re-collapses. And we can see it with high-speed photography, and it's very interesting. I think people think of it as little explosions, but it's really a quick foam collapse. And it's very, very gentle, it's not violent. So that's the basis of how popcorn works.

And then of course, there is a lot of chemistry that's going on. So the Maillard reaction and caramelization of sugars, that's what's giving it that smell and that color. The ideal popcorn should be a light yellow color. If it's too dark, then it will taste bitter, and it will also be more brittle, and it will break easier. So it's really delicate. And I love popcorn, I mean, this is my favorite snack. But I think that it's nice that popcorn is the seed of the plant, it's the seed of corn. And you get this whole fluffy foam structure that's very light and very crispy and very tasty. And it's really exciting.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book in the bread rack.

It was always the same one: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, library stamp from a town forty miles away. She would set it on the flour bin, wipe butter from the cover, and mean to take it back after her shift. By noon, the errands and heat and sleep would swallow the thought.

Then, next Thursday, there it would be again, tucked between cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hummed with the proofing cabinet and the old radio’s static. Rain pressed silver lines down the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons.

She opened it.

In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

Mara turned to page 47. A grey heron stood in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once.

Mara brushed flour from her apron, unlocked the front door, and turned on the little OPEN sign.

Question: Why is the history of math so separated from math itself in education? Wouldn't it be more interesting if this weren't the case?
items.raw:
Hi Sam,

Thanks for your message. Great question. I think education maths is very results oriented, in the sense that it's important to know that $2+2=4$, or that $\sqrt{4}=2$. So it's not like history, which you learn chronologically. You learn history chronologically but maths is more of a tree, so you need to learn things in order and people often miss the story of it. There's many books that incorporate the story into the maths, for example Hardy and Wright's Introduction to the Theory of Numbers is a really nice book that gives the history and then follows with the proofs. I think if you approach teaching maths that way, it's more interesting for the learners but at the same time it's harder to do curriculum and grading and so on. So I think it's a totally just critique of the current educational system. But yeah, it is more interesting to see a problem in context and then solve it.

Cheers,
Rob

Chris

Question: Why does metal react so violently when microwaved?
items.raw: When metal is microwaved, the electric field from the radiation causes free electrons in the metal to move about randomly, or jiggle. That induces a current, that creates a lot of spark or arcing. Especially at the sharp edges and points, the current density becomes very large. So the arcing is more. And that creates a very high local temperature, causing sparks and even fires. And in some cases, even causing the metal to melt or burn. So that's why we try to avoid putting metal inside the microwave cavity.

A simple rain gauge measures rainfall by catching precipitation in a funnel and directing it into a cylindrical measuring tube. 

To ensure accurate and easy reading, the gauge's top opening is deliberately wider than the inner measuring tube. This difference in diameter acts as an amplifier. For example, if the collection opening has ten times the area of the inner tube, one inch of rainfall will fill the tube to a height of ten inches. Another major source is wind exposure. Strong winds can create turbulence around the gauge's mouth, carrying raindrops over the opening and causing the instrument to underestimate the actual rainfall.

Question: Why is the USA drinking age set at 21 when in most other respects you're an adult at 18.
items.raw: I think there's two factors at play here. The first is cultural and the second is actuarial. In terms of culture, it's important to understand that drinking is very special to Americans. People often romanticize drinking, they drink to celebrate, they drink to mourn, and we tend to celebrate holidays, football games, birthdays, Thanksgiving, Christmas, graduations, basically every important thing we do in our lives is associated with alcohol. So it's important in many ways to not make it the first drink. That's the cultural side. And also because of the scary car crash statistics in the 80s and early 90s. People who are between 18 and 21 tend to have more car accidents than people above 21 or below 18. So that really sparked this change. And it was a totally arbitrary decision, it could be 20, it could be 23, it could be 25. But 21 is a culturally significant age in the US. Twenty-first birthday parties are huge. You're going to drink all night, you're going to have this massive celebration. So 21 is kind of a natural age to try to put the voting age and the drinking age in sync. Now in the actuarial sense, it turns out that driving statistics say it's actually lower in 18 than 21. But again, it's just the general brain development that says, well, people aren't fully grown and rational at 18. They're still developing. Their frontal lobe isn't fully developed. They're still impulsive. And so in many, many other cultures, we tend to have the drinking age much lower. And in fact, the drinking age in France is 16. In Germany and many other countries, it's 18. But the United States is particularly, I think, conservative when it comes to drinking. Just the historical baggage that we've brought with us from the teetotalers and the puritans and so on. That's why we are somewhat special in terms of drinking age.

Question: Why is the USA drinking age set at 21 when in most other respects you're an adult at 18.
items.raw: I think it is a bizarre compromise. It's almost certainly the liquor lobby. In the mid seventies, when a whole lot of states lowered their drinking age to 18, and then 19 and 20, there was a huge increase in teenage auto accident death rates, and the insurance and liquor industries were horrified. So the liquor industry very smartly said, you know, we want you to drink liquor, but we don't want to be sued every time some drunk 18 year old goes and wrecks a car and kills somebody. So they pushed for a federal compromise. So there was a law passed in 1984, it was the minimum drinking age law, which said that if a state wanted to tax interstate commerce of alcohol, that is, wanted to sell alcohol across state lines, they had to raise their drinking age to 21. So most states raised their drinking age to 21, and then there's a little bunch of states, Mississippi for instance, that really don't really care about interstate commerce of alcohol. It has a drinking age of 18. But most states raised it to 21. So it's really more of a highway safety issue. They didn't raise it because 21 year olds are less drunk than 18 year olds, they raised it because they were less likely to die in an accident. So it's a very weird compromise and something that the American establishment has sort of calcified around. They're very reluctant to change it. But I think the argument for lowering it is pretty strong. The sophistication gap between 18 and 21 is very large. People become legal voters at 18, they become legal adults in pretty much all other respects. And the number of people between 18 and 21 who drink illegally is huge, and it creates this weird legal limbo where you're treated like an adult in most respects but like a child in drinking.

Question: Why is the USA drinking age set at 21 when in most other respects you're an adult at 18.
items.raw: It's a historical accident that has got ratcheted into law at the federal level. It wasn't always 21. In the early part of the 20th century it was 21 in some states, but then many of them lowered it. And then came the microbrewery revolution of the 1970s, and more and more states started lowering it to 18. And the tie to 21 came with the National Minimum Drinking Age Act of 1984, which said that if the drinking age is not 21, the state forfeits 10% of its federal highway funding. And the reason it was passed at 21 is because drunk driving was killing a huge number of people at the time, and there was huge pressure on Congress and state governments to do something about it. And they didn't actually look at the research of who is in drunk driving accidents, who is in drunk driving fatalities. They just had this assumption that the lower the drinking age, the more people drink, the more people get in cars, the more drunk driving. And so they set it at 21. But when you look at the data, in a lot of the European countries that have lower drinking ages, they actually have lower drunk driving fatalities than the US, so it's not that super great a correlation. There is some data that suggests that people have a lower risk of DUIs when they can drink socially, in a bar, in a club, where they can be monitored and it's a little more safe, and they can develop the social skills for moderating themselves and choosing when to drink. That may be one reason. We also have the argument that the brain does not finish developing until 25, so we argue, why are we going to start letting them drink at 18 and not wait until 25? But then again, we don't wait until 25 to let them drive cars or vote or fight wars, so it's a little strange that we only apply the criterion that the brain is not fully developed to alcohol.

Question: What's the difference between tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons etc?
items.raw:
Tornado, hurricane, typhoon, cyclone, and similar regional words all refer to intense, rotating air masses that form around a center of low pressure. The main distinction between these terms is largely geographical. When we talk about Atlantic and Northeast Pacific hurricanes, we refer to the same system that in the North Pacific, North Indian Ocean, and Bay of Bengal is called a typhoon. In the South Pacific and Indian Ocean, the same system is called a tropical cyclone. The South Pacific Australian States call it a willy-willy, and in South Africa, it's called a willy-willy or danda. Whatever the name, they are functionally very similar.

Then there is the tornado. Tornadoes are very much different. They are very tight, very narrow, very intense rotating air masses that are able to touch the ground. Tornadoes are often spawned from thunderstorms, thunderstorms called supercells. But they don't necessarily have to be spawned from supercells. They can happen in winter, in front of cold fronts. They can be very short-lived, they can last two minutes or they can last an hour, two hours, or in rare cases, several hours. And the damage they cause can be very severe, very concentrated, very localized. Whereas hurricanes or typhoons, they tend to be much broader. And they're not even touching the ground necessarily. A hurricane, a typhoon, is a tropical cyclone. And it forms over warm ocean waters, needs warm ocean waters to develop and sustain itself. It loses strength or dissipates over land. So it's more of an oceanic thing. Whereas tornadoes are mainly a land thing. They can form over lakes, over bays, over oceans, but they're mainly a land thing. So they're actually quite different.

One last term to mention is very common is the maelstrom, or the waterspout. A waterspout is basically a tornado, a vortex, that is over water. It can be a tornado that's over water. Or it can be a tropical tornado that's not as intense and not as organized, not as tight, not as narrow, but it's still over water. But it's the same principle. So tornadoes, waterspouts, hurricane, typhoon, cyclone. Different names, and the physics is actually very similar. But tornadoes are much more intense, much more concentrated, much more localized, and they touch the ground. Whereas hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones, do not necessarily touch the ground. And they're much broader and less intense, but they're longer lasting, they're better organized, they're broader.

items.raw: Tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons, and tropical depressions are all intense atmospheric phenomena, but they differ in scale, location, structural composition, and causation. We first need to distinguish tornadoes from other named storms. Tornadoes are not restricted to any particular geographic region or weather pattern. They are extremely localized spinning columns of dense air. Very often tornadoes form under supercell thunderstorms, but they can also form in a squall line or even very rarely out of a hurricane. The size of a tornado, from its bottom to its top, is typically hundreds of meters, maximum thousands of meters in length. The diameter of a tornado is often just a few tens of meters in size, but they can be hundreds of meters or even a few kilometers for very strong tornadoes. In contrast, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons are the same category of storm, just different names depending on where they occur. For instance, in the North Atlantic and Northeast Pacific we have hurricanes, in the Northwest Pacific we have typhoons. In the South Pacific, North Indian Ocean, and Southeast Indian Ocean we call them cyclones. And in the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea we call them simply cyclonic storms or cyclones. These storms are the tropical counterpart of temperate mid-latitude lows, which are storms that happen in the mid-latitudes in the non-tropical zone. So hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones are systems that originate in the tropical zone, which is around the equator, roughly between 30 degrees north and 30 degrees south. They are vast atmospheric systems that are several hundreds of kilometers or thousands of kilometers in diameter. Their rotation is always cyclonic, so in the Northern Hemisphere they rotate anticlockwise, and in the Southern Hemisphere they rotate clockwise. Their structure is very simple. It has a clear eye, and around that eye, it has a very intense rain and wind area called the eyewall. That's very typical to these storms. And as a by-product of the rotation and the velocity of the air, we often see very characteristic spiral arms, the spiral rain bands that are streaming outward from the eyewall. The typical lifespan of a hurricane or a typhoon or a cyclone is several days, maybe up to two weeks. Tornadoes typically only last a couple of minutes, up to maximum one or two hours. So that's the main difference. But the more important distinction is the energy source. Hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons are powered by the warm sea surface temperature. So you need very warm sea water, above 26 or 27 degrees, and you need a lot of moisture in the air. That's why hurricanes and cyclones form mostly over warm waters. Whereas tornadoes are powered by the gradient between the air temperature at the surface and the air temperature at altitude. So if we have very unstable air, the air is very warm and moist near the surface, and then at altitude we have very cold air, then we can create very unstable conditions, very strong updrafts that favor tornado formation.

Question: Can someone explain Post-Modernism like I'm 5, please?
items.raw:
I hate people who say postmodernism means everything is subjective and therefore all views are equal. That's not right. I think postmodernism is actually about humility and doubt and questioning. There is something that deeply resonates in postmodernism, which is the deconstruction of the narrative. We live in a constructed world and we tend to take that for granted. We tend to see what we see and the reality that's been constructed and think that's reality. And then postmodernism says, "Hey, let's take a step back and deconstruct this narrative. Look at the underside of it. See who's doing the construction and how they construct it and why. Why is this the way it is? What is being left out? What is being excluded?" So, it's actually a really critical and skeptical look at things. It doesn't mean that nothing is real, that there is no truth, it's just saying let's really look at all the angles and see how all these stories and narratives get constructed.

A good example of postmodernism is the way we view Hollywood films now, the canon of what makes a good movie, is postmodern in the sense that we have really lost the early 20th century obsession with realistic film. So now we have very fantastical movies that are making lots of money, but they're not really trying to tell you what real life is. They are trying to give you some postmodern kind of existential, magical realism or fantasy. And that's postmodern. When you deconstruct reality, the stuff that's real in the real world is only some tiny fraction of what's real. There's imaginary things, there's fantasy, there's dreams, there's ideas, there's thoughts. So, we stop being so obsessed with the realism of narrative. We are actually more comfortable with fantastical movies. So, that's the deconstruction of the narrative. So, it's a very interesting area of thought, and I think it's very useful to be postmodern in the sense that you're not just taking what's given to you at face value. And you're not letting people convince you that this narrative is the only narrative, the one and true narrative. But there's different narratives. And also postmodernism is very self-reflexive. It's very self aware. It's like, "Yeah, I am aware of what I am doing. I am aware that I'm constructing this narrative in this specific way." And it's really beautiful when writers do that. I really appreciate self-reflexive writing that's very self aware that it is constructing a narrative and it doesn't take it for granted. That's very postmodern. I really love that.

Question: Can someone explain Post-Modernism like I'm 5, please?
items.raw:
I think people get post-modernism pretty wrong. The popular modern take on post-modernism is that "there's no truth, reality, correctness, nothing, nothing real." But that's not really what post-modernism is. I think post-modernism has an important critique that the age of modernity, early 1900s, what we call high modernism, was very absolutist. That the history, universal history, was moving in a straight line towards progress, that Western civilization was moving in a straight line towards progress, towards truth, towards God, towards Enlightenment, towards democracy, towards science, towards progress. And there was this grand vision of what humanity would eventually look like. Post-modernism very rightly criticizes the arrogance, the confidence of that. It says, hold on, what about all the other people who we don't see, whose truth and reality are not captured by this Western, masculine, very Eurocentric vision of what progress means? And it also says, hold on, maybe modernity has more cracks than we think. Like religion, we said, oh, it's a dying idea. Religion's not dead at all. It's very very alive. So we've overestimated the progress that we're making. And then post-modernism also criticizes the idea of a universal language. Universal discourse. That a Frenchman and a woman from Bangladesh have exactly the same language, and have the same categories to explain the world. And it says, no, no, no. They're very different, and they have very different categories to explain their world.

So post-modernism is really the very valid critique of the arrogance of modernity. But I think post-modernism went very, very far, as in any critique, and ended up going too far. And I think it is actually very silly to say that the man walking in the forest and the man walking in the city, they see the same tree. Post-modernism is true in the fact that the city man sees a tree with a commercial value, economic value, that's very different than the man in the forest who sees the tree with something spiritual, something a lot more personal. So the tree is not the same. But then post-modernism takes this to the extreme that even the man in the forest, his tree is just another socially constructed tree. And then I think that post-modernism goes too far. But I think we still need post-modernism. We need that critique. We need that humility to say that we're not the only ones, we're not the only ones to define what reality, truth, progress mean, and that there are other voices that we need to pay attention to.

And then, postmodernism also doesn't think that there's just one architecture. There's just one way to view the world or just one way to approach life. There are many different ways. We just have to say, hey, everybody is different. We have a spectrum of truths. We have a spectrum of views, and they're all equally valid. That's not what we used to do. So eventually either it hits a plateau where there's no more potential recruitment, or the rate of growth of the recruitment becomes less than the rate of growth of the withdrawals. And then the balloon blows up and everything goes to zero. So all pyramid schemes in the end are doomed to collapse and blow up. But the early entrants do make money. They don't just suck value from existing players, but they actually create value. They make money.

Question: Theoretically, shouldn't a pyramid scheme work?
items.raw: A pyramid scheme theoretically works in the same way as compound interest or exponential growth. In a very hypothetical scenario with infinite supply of new entrants and infinite time, every person in the pyramid would end up getting paid based on recruiting new people, and those would then recruit new ones and so on. So the money would just trickle down and everybody would get paid, and the pyramid would be infinitely broad. But the reality is more cruel. The number of people on earth is limited, so we only have a limited supply of recruits. Also, we cannot recruit one person twice, or in other words, nobody can join two pyramids at once. So we are working with a limited pool of people. Meaning that eventually the funnel of people is reduced to zero, then pyramid collapses, and everybody at the very bottom is gonna lose their money.

Question: How does Winamp generate its visualisations?
items.raw: Winamp actually just does a DFT of the current audio stream, in realtime, and saves the power of each frequency band to a spectrum array. So that's that for the spectrum visualisations, you're getting a standard spectrum analyser. The 3D ball and the fish tank are quite different, they do a raytrace rendering of a fractal in realtime. So they are generating a 3D model of the fractal, and basically raycasting the camera through the fractal, and seeing what hits and doing diffuse lighting on it. So it's expensive but surprisingly cool. They have the whole model and just rotate it around in realtime, doing the raytracing. The fractal is generated based on the audio, so what you see is a huge solid fractal kind of object, and then the camera moves through it. So if it's really low frequencies or silence or something, the camera is outside the fractal and you see the black screen. But as soon as a frequency hits, then the fractal just grows, and it becomes denser, and then the camera will move through the fractal. And you see the colours. And in the fish tank, there's also these fish that are also purely random generated fractals, and then you just see them swimming through this fractal solid. And it's really beautiful and impressive. Very impressive for 1997, and even today it's pretty cool. As long as you remember that it's a raytraced fractal. It's not a 3D model that you see in Blender or Maya, or a mesh that's generated. It's fractal generated. And the raytracing just goes through the fractal. So it's not a fractal mesh, it's just the fractal equation. And then when the camera shoots out a ray, it just traces the fractal function and sees what it hits. That's why it's raytraced, that's why it's slow. But today it's not bad. We render realtime fractal raytraced stuff in game engines, actually. I don't know, Unreal or something, I'm not sure. I think Unreal does actually. But it's very efficient, very efficient raytracing. But it's quite clever. And also, Winamp took the CPU power of the audio thread, and used that to generate a spectrum, and then passed the spectrum to the visualisation thread, that was rendering the fractal. So they're running the fractal render in a separate thread, so it didn't get hitched, didn't stutter. So that's clever, that's quite clever.

Question: How does Winamp generate its visualisations?
items.raw: What is happening in Winamp visualizations is actually fairly simple and it all starts with a very simple first step, which is to take the audio, and convert it to the frequency domain. So, you look at the audio, and you basically take one time domain sample, and you look at the spectrum that is contained within that sample. There are different ways of doing this, different FFT transforms, or fast Fourier transforms. Winamp does it in the Fourier domain. And, once you have that spectrum, you have all the frequencies represented. So, now you can generate a visualization, for example, spectrum analyzer, very easily. And then the information is stored in a memory, and updated every few milliseconds. And then, when you go to render it, you can do very complex things, very easily, just by looking at the memory, and painting the visualization, in whatever way you want, for example, draw it along the edges of a circle, draw it in a spectrum analyzer, etc. That's pretty easy. But what's very interesting is that Winamp is, or was, more complex than that. Winamp has some more visualizations. It has GoGo, for example. GoGo does not really look at the frequency domain at all, it looks at the time domain. It looks at the raw audio sample, and reacts to it. And so, what happens is it looks at the variance of the samples. So, if it's very quiet, there's very little variance, and if it's very loud, very, very noisy, there's a lot of variance. So, it's basically just measuring the noise, or the loudness of the music. And then it takes that information, and uses it as a movement generator. It moves around random particles on the screen, and the speed of their movement is determined by the noise or the loudness of the music. So, if you play something very quiet, it moves very slow. If you play something very noisy, very loud, it moves very fast. And so, you get this cool moving particles visualization, that doesn't necessarily have anything to do with the spectrum or the frequency. It's really just using time domain as a movement generator. And then there's others, things that are sort of in between. Things that take the frequency domain, but use it to modify, or change, the time domain visualization. Question: How does Winamp generate its visualisations?
items.raw: Winamp's visualizations are generally speaking highly analytically based. Essentially, the audio is compressed into frequency band data, and a lot of the visualization are basically just drawing of that frequency data, especially the ones that show bars or circles. These just color them differently or make them look a little more organic. And for those that are oriented around shapes and then also, things like making a space kind of moving around, these usually are more heuristic. I mean, it's not terribly clever actually. They just draw some very simple geometric shapes in some weird manner. And then they rotate the whole thing, do some transformations to make it kind of move around, move up and down, zoom in and out, and whatnot. And then they also color it depending on how loud that band is or how loud the overall music is. So it's very simple, but it still does the job. So people still love it. We have drawn on these ideas in different ways, but very similar. So in practice, the basic idea of Winamp visualizations is we have a spectrum analyser that is going to give us frequency bands and basically we then draw these as just bars, or we draw them as a polygon, a circle. And then we just color them. And then for some of the ones that are more space-oriented, we basically draw something that has little relationship to the actual spectrum, and we just use spectrum as some sort of color or lightness value. And then just rotate it and transform it. That's basically all of it. So it's not scientific visualization that is like precise and meaningful. It's just decoration. And then, of course, some of the visualization plugins out there, ones that are more modern, ones that try to be more modern and 3D and things like that, they actually, I think they use actual frequency values as kind of height values. Like actual 3D topography. They have, like, a base and then they draw mountains out of the spectrum, so it's more meaningful. But it's still not a really meaningful visualization, in terms of that we would actually use it to see the spectrum, because it's just too cluttered and too much geometry, and it's not very easy to read. So it's really very surface-level visualization.

At 3:17 a.m., the bakery was all yeast and silence. Marisol slid the first loaves into the oven and found it again: a worn paperback, *The Borrowers*, resting in the wicker basket by the back door. Every Thursday for six weeks, someone had returned it here instead of the library two blocks over. No name. No card. Just the book, smelling faintly of rain and woodsmoke.

Tonight a folded note was tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her floury hands and opened it. *I can't make it to the library before closing. Please keep it another week. I like knowing it's warm.*

Marisol looked at the basket, then at the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing. She wrapped it in wax paper, tucked the note back into the book, and set both by the door. Then she flipped the sign to OPEN and started the coffee.
